newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe public health sector under siege.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe public health sector under siege.

text.p: Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe has over the past 16 years heralded his country's public health sector as one of his government's major success stories since it came into power in 1980.

But that success is fast losing its glow after unprecedented strikes by health workers which they say signal mounting frustration over deteriorating standards in government hospitals and government inaction to stem the slide.

In the three-week strike by health workers which has led to closure of Zimbabwe's two largest hospitals, the government blames junior doctors and nurses for being greedy, saying it spends about 49 percent of gross domestic product on wages for them and other public servants.
The strikers say their stoppage is not only for higher pay and better working conditions, but also to draw the government's attention to falling standards in its hospitals.
It is the second stoppage after a three-week strike by a majority of civil servants in September, also over wages. The government then awarded all its workers a 20 percent rise.
"The government believes that we are only striking for more money but the truth of the matter is we are also fed up with the situation in the hospitals," said one striking junior doctor.

"Things are bad. Standards have been going down over the years and the government doesn't seem to care. That's what's frustrating," said a striking nurse who said she had witnessed the changes in the past 10 years.
Doctors, nurses and consultants tell the same tale of shortages of essential drugs, protective clothing, basic equipment and staff.
Hospital authorities refused to comment.

"The shortages are the most frustrating to deal with in this job. Most times there are no drugs. A doctor prescribes a drug but it's not available in the hospital so nurses have to improvise," said one nurse who refused to be named.

"Sometimes we have no gloves to protect ourselves from infectious diseases, so what are we supposed to do when an HIV- infected patient comes with a wound? Of course I cannot refuse to treat him but I am risking infection," she said.
A junior doctor who also refused to be named said he refused to handle without gloves any patient with an open wound.
"We also do not have facial masks to wear when we handle TB patients. The number of nurses who are dying from infections through lack of protective clothing is frightening," charged another nurse.
"Sometimes we don't even have soap to wash our hands and the patients' bed linen and other clothing. There's also a shortage of bed linen for the patients," added another.
"To all that, add the meagre salaries we get, poor working conditions including the long hours. It adds up to frustration."
Statistics show government hospitals are losing experienced staff to private clinics and surgeries at the rate of 30 a month due to poor working conditions and lack of incentives.
Nurses earn on average about Z$2,800 (U.S. $263) net, including allowances, per month, while junior doctors get around Z$3,000 and consultants gross about 12,500.

The government says it has fired 1,000 of 14,000 state-employed nurses and 100 of 800 doctors involved in the strike, and is looking for replacements in Britain, South Africa and other African countries.

The government has conceded that all is not well in the public health sector. Health and Child Welfare Minister Timothy Stamps early this year laid most of the blame on the World Bank, which he said had pressed for cuts in the budget for social services.
For weeks last year, some state hospitals were asking patients to bring their own food and linen after private companies cut off supplies, citing mounting debts.
The situation has slightly improved, medical staff say.
($1=10.6 Zimbabwe dollars)
